Another cowardly deed, committed as usual by a negro ruffian, occurred yesterday morning on the Poplar street boulevard, opposite the residence of Col. H. A. Montgomery. The scene of the probable murder was the little grocery of John Genochio, an Italian, over seventy years old. This old fellow has been peculiarly unfortunate. Among the negroes his wealth has been considered something fabulous, and thus he has been an object of cupidity. A few years ago he and his wife were both assaulted and robbed. The assault committed yesterday will in all likelihood bring about the old man's death. About 10 o'clock

A NEGRO ROUSTABOUT
and hard citizen generally named Alfred Ross came into the store and called for several articles. He purchased twenty-five cents worth of sugar and twenty-five cents worth of coffee. Then he called for ten cents worth of nails. The old man stooped down to get them, and while he was bent over Ross made a murderous assault upon him with a large rock he held in his hand. The rock broke all to pieces, and the blood spurted from the old man's head and he fell senseless to the floor. The negro.

WAS GETTING READY TO STEAL
when some one was heard by him approaching. He accordingly ran hurriedly from the grocery. As he went in and as he went out of the store he was seen by a colored boy who is in the employ of Colonel Montgomery. The news of the attempted murder flew rapidly, and soon a body of men were out in pursuit of the negro. He ran so rapidly that some of his pursuers seeing the impossibility of overtaking on foot, got their horses. When he saw that he began jumping fences. He ran like a scared deer, and it seemed as if nothing daunted him. Over fences, rough fields and roads he ran without hesitation. When he was finally captured, he was panting like a brute at bay, and

NEARLY ALL HIS CLOTHES
had been torn from him. The sight of a pistol, displayed by his nearest pursurer, caused him to surrender without resistance. He ran over a mile before he was caught. He is now in the stationhouse. He stoutly maintained his innocence when questioned. He states that he came in on the Halliday and put up at his home on Commerce and Main. When asked why he had gone out on the boulevard, he said he and his wife had had a fuss and he had gone out in the country because she had had a warrant sworn out against him. When questioned as to the cause of

HIS LIGHTNING FLIGHT,
he said he wasn't going to stand still when men were coming at him with pistols. He was frightened into running. Chief Davis went to see Ross's wife, and she denied that they had ever had any quarrel at all, or that she had any intention of getting out a warrant. She said she had threatened to do so some time ago if he didn't give her money with which to support herself. She said further in support of her statement, that Ross staid with her Sunday night.

THE CONDITION OF THE OLD MAN
is very critical. Dr. Willett was summoned to his side, and he pronounced the wounds very serious. The fact that Genochio is seventy or seventy-five years old, and the fact that he lost a great deal of blood render his recovery extremely doubtful. The blow was a terrible one. It will go hard with the negro if the case proves a fatal one.

Beyond a Doubt as the Man who Assaulted Genochio.
The evidence against Alfred Ross for assaulting old man Genochio was so convincing when he was called this morning that the attorney for the defense did not produce any testimony whatever, and the prisoner was bound over. Old man Genochio appeared in court with his head bandaged and was positive as to the identity of the prisoner with the man who struck him. He was supported by four others, who were equally certain that Ross was the guilty man. His attorney resorted to a neat little dodge, which, however, failed to do his case any good. Ross was rigged up in an entirely different suit from that worn when the crime was committed. He is a splendidly formed darky, of a rather striking appearance, and looks like a dare devil criminal. COLEMAN, April 8.—District court is in session.

FROM GEORGETOWN.

Austin Presbytery in Session... Was Never More Prosperous.

Special Telegram to the Examiner.

GEORGETOWN, April 8.—The Presbytery of Austin met at Georgetown on Thursday, at 7 p.m. A large attendance of ministers and elders were present. Rev. W.B. Bloys, of Coleman City, was elected moderator, and Rev. McClelland, of Brownwood, secretary. Two new churches were reported organized; also a large increase of membership and attendance on public worship in various churches. There are no unemployed ministers and now no unsupplied charge in the Presbytery. The Presbytery never was so strong or working in such a flourishing condition as now.

JACK WHARTON.

His Sudden Death, Friday.

Special Telegram to the Post.

NEW ORLEANS, April 7.—United State8 Marshal Jack Wharton died suddenly at 5 p. m., in an apoplectic fit. At about 3 p. m. he went into the office of Surveyor of the Port Pinchback, in the custom-house, and was talking with T. B. Stamps, a colored man and local politician. He complained of having a headache and of feeling hot, and asked to have the window opened and laid himself down on the sofa. Stamps noticed a change in his face and called Pinchback. Wharton looked up to Pinchback and said: "I am gone," and went off in a fit. Physicians were summoned, but could do nothing. He lay unconscious for two hours and then passed away.

FROM TURNERSVILLE.

Crop Prospects and Current News Items.

TURNERSVILLE, April 7.—The crop prospects are somewhat improved. Wheat has suffered seriously from rust, but is now coming out. In some instances, however, it still looks very sickly. The best planters in this section estimate from present prospects, about half a crop of wheat and full oat crop. Corn planting is about done, and cotton planting progressing. Some corn is up and looking well.

His father has been telegraphed for from Rockdale, and has arrived to see to his son's case. It is said that his father has fled an affidavit of his son's insanity. Prot. Dick Batsell, colored, who is wanted both here and in Sherman to answer for burglaries he committed, was shot last night in Stringtown by Police Officer Clapp, about 9 o'clock, and it is thought that he is mortally wounded. He is the party who burglarized Mrs. Carleton's residence of a lot of jewelry, which was subsequently recovered from a pawn-shop. The officers were unable to meet up with him until last night, and when he saw them, broke and ran for the brush, followed by Officers Clapp and Ed Cornwall, who overtook the fugitive, who resisted arrest, when the officer struck him a blow over the head with a pistol, falling him to the ground. As he arose he struck at the officer with a soda-water bottle, and seeing it gleam in the dark, the officer, mistaking it for a pistol, fired on him and at the same instant Batse'l staggered and fell, but recovering himself, he hobbled into the brush, crawling a part of the time on his hands and knees. They procured lights and searched in vain for him, but he could not be found. The brush is very dense and the ground very rugged at that point. Clapp shot at his body with a large Colt's pistol, which is likely to produce death. The search for him will be resumed this morning.

CIRCASSIAN ASSASSINS.

Cairo, April 12.—The Circassian officers arrested in connection with the plot to assassinate the minister of war numbered sixteen. Dissatisfaction at non-promotion actuated them.

POLISH DISTRICT MARSHALS.

St. Petersburg, April 12.—That Poland may be represented at his coronation the Czar has appointed ten Polish district Marshals. A district marshal has not existed in Poland since 1863.

IN HONOR OF PARNELL.

Cork, April 12.—Bands are playing, houses illuminated and crowds parading the streets in honor of the release of Parnell.

Revolution in Hayti.

Havana, April 12.—A revolution began in the capital of Hayti on the night of the 26th of March. Gonaives, of Port au Prince, and son entered the movement. Martial law was proclaimed and President Solomon is preparing to march to Cape Hayti with 3,000 men.

Laud League Convention.

Washington, April 12.—Committees of the Land League convention on resolutions and organization were to-day appointed. John Boyle, of Boston, offered a resolution which recites the fact of the imprisonment of American prisoners in English jails, quotes the Land League and dispatches of Minister Low-

ell and calls upon the president to immediately recall Lowell and provides for the presentation of the resolution to President Arthur by a committee. The resolution was unanimously adopted amidist great applause. The committee on credentials reported 227 delegates present.

Two More of the Golden City's Victims.

Memphis, Tenn., April 12.—Two more bodies lost by the disaster were discovered this afternoon four miles below here. One has been identified as Robert Kelly, second engineer of the ill-fated vessel, who remained so calm at his post until the steamer had been made fast to the coal fleet. The other body is an unknown dead passenger about thirty-five years of age. He had on three shirts and grey pants. Both had met death by drowning.

A Fiendish Outrage.

Fort Worth, Texas, April 12.—Saturday night Bill Jackson, a negro, broke into a room occupied by the 15 year old daughter of Mr. Henderson, who lives a mile and a half south of this city, and after choking her until she was insensible outraged her. The parents were attracted to the room by a gasping sound, when they found the shocking fate of their daughter. Officers were at once put on the scoundrel's tracks.

Dead Dink.

Dallas, Tex., April 12.—Policeman Charles Clapp to-night attempted to arrest Dink Batsel, a notorious and desperate negro burglar, for whom the authorities have been watching several weeks. Clapp discovered him in a dark part of the negro quarter. The burglar attempted to resist him with a soda-water bottle, which Clapp mistook for a pistol, he fired, inflicting what is supposed to be a fatal wound.

Sweet Scented Swindler.

"The Last Rose of Summer."

The Adams Express company received a telegram yesterday morning from the Pittsburgh and Fort Wayne train which left here at 9 o'clock the previous evening for the East, that a man had been found concealed in a box in the express car and had been handed over to the officers at Van Wert, Ind. He gave his name as John McAuley, of 191 West Monroe street. The box, which was provided with wire at the top and bottom to give ventilation, was labelled "The Last Rose of Summer," and the expressmen supposed it contained flowers, but when Mr. McAuley was found snugly ensconced in it, they fancied they had captured a robber. He had with him a supply of provisions sufficient to last six days, and from the information gleaned, it was concluded that the man had adopted this novel way of traveling to save the difference between the passenger and freight rates of fare, the latter having been prepaid to Philadelphia. It is understood that Mr. McAuley is about sixty-five years of age and in comfortable circumstances, but given to eccentricities which have often set his family on their wits' end. It is said that if he had succeeded in reaching the City of Brotherly Love in his box he intended to undertake a similar trip to Denver, Col. It was lucky for Mr. McAuley that this attempt to reach the Atlantic seaboard as an express package was discovered in the daytime, for if he had been found in the night the express messenger would have been likely to have peppered him with a revolver. It is to be regretted that the agent, after satisfying himself that the man in the box was harmless, did not allow him to proceed in his novel conveyance merely for the purpose of testing a man's powers of endurance for two days and a night for the purpose of evading the expense of a few paltry dollars, and in order to give the sleepy Philadelphia papers a sensation. But the gentleman's scheme was nipped in the bud, and the company may require him to prove his object was not robbery. —Chicago Tribune.

The Aquidneck Assault Case.
LEWERT B. L. Oct 13—Wm H. Tew
The Aquidneck Assault Case.
NEWPORT, R. I., Oct. 13.—Wm. H. Tew, the police officer who beat a boy at Aquidneck fair on Thursday, was brought to court to-day. He pleded not guilay and was sent to jaff to await trial next Tuesday.
george-h-tew-newport-1882-10-12.A8:
THE Ballon House, at North Adams, Mass., was fired by an incendiary the other morning. A fireman and a lady boarder were hurt.

STRONG re-inforcements have been sent to Southern Tunis, with the object of carrying on operations on a large scale against insurgents during the cold season.

REPRESENTATIVE LOWE, of Alabama, died at Huntsville, Oct. 12.

ALONZO W. SLAYBACK, a prominent attorney, was shot and killed by John A. Cockerill, editor of the Post-Dispatch, in St. Louis, Mo., Oct. 18. Witnesses give different versions of the affair, but it is understood that Mr. Slayback, accompanied by a friend, visited the editor's sanctum to demand satisfaction for an editorial publication. Mr. Cockerill gave himself up.

JOHN ALBERT, the constable who shot down a boy he wanted to arrest, near Toronto, Canada, is to be hanged November 10.

SIDNEY WRIGHT, a farm hand, was fatally injured by runaway horses near Bloomington, Ill., on the 12th.

An attempt to lynch a young man named G. H. Tew, who thought it part of his duty as a special policeman to use his club on a boy, caused much excitement near Newport, R. I., the other day. Tew sought refuge in a farm-house, and the timely arrival of a police force saved him.

ALBERT JONES, a miller in San Saba County, Texas, was killed by De Witt Jolly in a quarrel over business matters the other night. The murderer escaped.

BOB TAYLOR, one of the Tennessee desperadoes who murdered Sheriff Hamilton and his deputy on the 14th of September, was shot dead by Sheriff R. P. Goodall, of Laclede County, Mo., on a train near Lebanon, Oct. 13. Taylor had been hiding in Missouri for some weeks. When ordered to surrender he drew his revolver, but the sheriff was too quick for him.

Two little daughters of Louis Wright were run down by a train at Natick, Mass., on the 13th, and fatally injured.

Hurd's elevator at Bridgeport, Conn., burned on the 13th. Loss, $135,000.

A HAND-CAR was run down by a train on the Sciota Valley road, near Chillicothe, Ohio, on the 12th. A laborer named Longman was killed and two others were seriously injured.

Some months ago William Kennock, a government detective, gained the confidence of a lot of counterfeiters in Tipton County, Ind., and was admitted to membership in the band. He got matters in shape the other night and fourteen of the coiners were arrested and taken to Indianapolis. Warrants have been issued for the arrest of half a dozen others.

Lizzie Jackson; a pretty girl of eighteen, hanged herself in a station-house at Chicago the other night.

EXECUTIONS on the 13th: William Austin, at Lancaster, Ky.; Paul Pringle, colored, Mansfield, La.

The strikers on the Northern Pacific Railroad in Montana having driven the Chinese from the works and threatened to hang Superintendent Hallet, United States soldiers have been dispatched to the scene and a conflict is anticipated.

George D. Rise, cashier of the bank at Lebanon, Pa., was knocked down and robbed of a sachel containing $30,000 the other evening. Mr. Rise had just brought the money from Philadelphia, and while on the way to the bank he was passed by two men, and directly afterward received a stunning blow, knocking him into the gutter. He held on to the sachel, and cried for help, but the robbers, after beating and kicking him, wrenched it from the handle and escaped.

MAGGIE O'NEAL made a savage attack upon Jane Bradt, in Sanford's mills, Amsterdam, N. Y., on the 12th, stabbing her twenty times with a pair of scissors.

A BRACE OF TRAGEDIFS
AT EVANSVILLE AND COLUMBUS.
A Whole Family Butchered and Mutilated-Four Arrests on Suspicion, but No Positive Proof.
A Step-son Plunges a Kulfe into the Heart of His Step-father.
Evansville, August 13.—A most horrid and brutal murder occurred this morning or during last night, in the northwestern part of the city. Alexander Wilbur, a German saloon keeper, his wife and his little son, seven years old, were found murdered in their house. The father and mother in their bed and the boy in the adjoining room. They were evidently killed while attempting escape. The heads of all three were crushed with a batchet and their throats cut and mangled in a most brutal manner. An infant of six months old was found, unharmed in its crib, smiling and crowing and unconscious of its bereavement. The most intense excitement prevails, and vigorous efforts are being made to discover the perpetrator or perpetrators of the flendish act. The furniture on the premises was scattered and thrown about promiscuously. Two drawers of a bureau were drawn out, while the middle one was found locked, and it contained $56 50. It is not believed the murderer or murderers got anything of value, if that was the object. Geo. Lenhart, Chas. W. Carter, Phil Voll and a disreputable young man named Jo Bird have been arrested on suspicion. About six years ago a man named Krugg was murdered on the premises by a negress named Leroy. Lenhart married his widow and wanted to occupy the premises, but Wilber had a long lease on the house and Lenhart has been heard to threaten to kill Wilber if he did not vacate. Carter and Voll were found leaving the city soon
and Lehart has been heard to threaten to kill Wilber if he did not vacate. Carter and Voll were found leaving the city soon after the murder was discovered, and Bird was arrested on general principles. Suspicion points most strongly to Lehart, who stoutly denies his guilt. The coroner has been investigating the horror, but has not returned a verdict.
george-lenhart-evansville.A9:
THE EVANSVILLE TRAGEDY.
Further Particulars of the Revolting Horror.
Further Particulars of the Revolting Horror.
Evansville, Aug. 14.—Further particulars in regard to the murder of the Weiber family show that robbery was committed in connection with it. A watch, two pistols, two pocket books, and some money were taken. The tracks of two men by a circuitous route were traced from Weiber's house to the river bank. Early Sunday morning two negroes were seen rowing rapidly down stream, and it is believed they were hired to do the deed. They have been followed down the river by a detective for a distance of 40 miles.
george-lenhart-evansville.A17:
The Evansville Horror.
EVANSVILLE, IND., August 16.—There were no new developments in the murder case to-day. The funeral this afternoon was very large. The bodies were viewed by thousands. Rev. Father Bultman, in his sermon, cautioned the people against mob law. Sheriff Kerth, in the silence of night, conveyed Lenhart to Booneville. When the citizens in the lower part of the city heard this they were very indignant. At a late hour a rumor has gained credence that a large body of men are congregating in German township to go horseback to Booneville to Lynch Lenhart. There is but little doubt but that this is true, as the people seem to be determined that Lenhart must hang. The wires are not working to Booneville, and the authorities can not be notified.
george-lenhart-evansville.A22:
CRIMES AND CASUALTIES.
EVANSVILLE, Ind., was intensely excited on the morning of the 13th by the discovery that Alexander Wieber, a German saloon-keeper, his wife and his little son, seven years old, had been butchered in bed. The heads of all three were crushed with a hatchet, and their throats were cut and mangled in a most brutal manner. An infant of six months was found unharmed in its crib, smiling and crowing, unconscious of bereavement. The house in which the tradegy was enacted was formerly owned by a German named Krugg, who was killed there about six years ago by negroes. His widow married George Lenhart, a German laborer, who has done little or no work since his marriage. He has frequently asked his wife to let him have the house and run a saloon, but as Wieber, the man who was murdered, had a lease on the house, she could not do it. Lenhart is an ignorant fellow, and believed himself aggrieved by Wieber's possession of the house. Frequently he
lead away from the house, made by a man with one shoe, and a sock on the other foot. Lenhart has a sore upon the instep of his left foot, and has walked without a shoe for some days in consequence. His tracks correspond with those found. He denies the commission of the crime. Charles W. Carter and Philip Voll were arrested about ten miles from the city. Carter was searched, and had in a pocket a razor covered with blood and a handkerchief spattered. Voll is but a boy, who had been looking for work and was going back to Mount Carmel. If the purpose of the murder was robbery it failed signally, for they got not a cent or a valuable, though several hundred dollars were concealed behind a drawer in the bureau.

John Jamison got tangled in the harness of a runaway horse near Dallas, Texas, the other day, and was kicked to death. Miss Louisa King was thrown out of the buggy and badly injured.

COMMITTING ARSON AND MURDER.
St. Louis, March 31.—The store of Joseph Yerger, postmaster, near Antonia, was set on fire on Thursday. When the family rushed from the burning building a shot was fired and Yerger fell and died. One Tressler is suspected of being the criminal.

TWO CATTLE THIEVES LYNCHED.
Denver, March 31.—A body of men took W. T. Plebus and Jav McGrew, two cattle thieves, from jail last night and hanged them to a tree near. The lynchers are believed to be members of the Cattle Growers' Protective Association.

DAMAGES FOR PERSONAL INJURY.
Detroit, March 31.—Thomas H. Rae, a switchman, has received a verdict for $6,000 against the Grand Trunk Railway Company for injuries sustained by him while in the discharge of his duties. He claimed that he was unditted by reason of disability for the duties given him, and that the company's agent knew of that fact.

ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER AND SUICIDE.
Cleveland, March 31.—Robert Bluen, a blacksmith, this morning fired twice at his wife, who was beside him in bed, inflicting dangerous wounds in her head. Mrs. Bluen fled. Bluen then placed the muzzle of his revoiver against his own forehead and blew his brains out. He was devoted to his wife. For three months he had been disabled by rheumatism, and it is supposed that he was deranged by pain and fear of poverty.

PITTSBURG, (Pa.,) April.—El Hanova Spring Hotel, at Hayville, was burned this morning. Loss, $138 000. Fortunately no boarders were in the house.

Wholesale Lynching of Cattle Thieves.

PUEBLO, Col., April 1.—Between 2 and 3 o'clock this morning a mob of sixteen men quietly took from the county jail two notorious cattle thieves, Phoebus and McGraw, and hung them to a tree on Santa Fe avenue, within 100 yards of the jail. There is an organization in the county known as the Cattle Growers Association, a branch of the State organization, and is composed of cattle growers for protection of their property. There is little or no doubt that the mob was composed of members of this organization. The lynchers next rode to a ranch ten miles miles away, surrounded the house and captured S. P. Chastine, Billy Chastine and Frank Owsley. Their hands were securely bound and they were put on horses and taken to a thick patch of timber and etrung up. There is but one of the gang left.

Discovery of a Great Pot of Old Money.

ST. LOUIS, April 1.—Two laborers, digging a drain on the premises of James E. Haggerty, on Collins street, to-day, unearthed a large pot tightly sealed which proved to contain a large amount of English sovereigns, American silver dollars and a lot of Continental currency. The money has not yet been counted, but there is probably from $20,000 to $30,000 of coin which is dated in the last century. The currency bears the date in 1777. The house was occupied by Montgomery Blair many years ago, but afterward passed into the possession of Samuel Gaty.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., March 31.—The confession of John Land, train robber, was given to the press today. It is the same as was anticipated in a previous dispatch, and inculpates the James boys, Miller, Little, Bugler, Cummings, Mott, Armstrong and Creed Chapman.

The Bodies on the Golden City.

MEMPHIS, April 1.—All hope of recovering the dead bodies from the wreck of the Golden City has been abandoned. No further attempt will be made until the river falls sufficiently to permit divers to work with some show of success.

Execution of a Nihilist.

NEW YORK, April 1.—The Herald's St. Petersburg dispatch says: Lieutenant Sonnowoff was shot this morning at Cronstadt, in the presence of the troops of the fortress. All other persons condemned at the recent Nihilist trial had their sentences commuted by the Emperor to an indefinite period of hard labor in the mines.

The Rowing Race Between Oxford and Cambridge.

LONDON, April 1.—In the race today the Oxford crew won by six boat lengths. The Cambridge crew was the first to come out on the river. They took the Middlesex side. The final betting was five to one on the Oxfords. The boats started at one minute past one o'clock. The Cambridges were the first to take water and immediately led by half a boat's length, but were caught and passed by the Oxford boat before fifty yards had been traversed. At the soap works, a mile and a half from the starting point, the Oxford crew were in the lead by three lengths. At Hammersmith Bridge, two furlongs further on, they were four lengths in front of the Cambridge crew, and off Cheswick Mall the latter seemed to be fairly done with. The Oxford crew finished in good form. They won as they pleased. The Cambridge men were exhausted at the finish and their rowing was irregular.

A QUIET LYRIC PARTY.
Sixteen Masked Cattle Dealers Hang Five Men to Trees in One Night
PUEBLO, Col., April 1 — W. F. Phoebus and A. W. J. McGraw, cattle thieves, were taken from the county jail here at 2 A. M., by a party of sixteen masked men belonging to the Cattle Drovers' Association, who received admittance on representing that they were Deputy Sheriffs with a prisoner and hanged them to a tree in Santa Fe avenue. The lynchers subsequently went to Reynolds' place on St. Charles road, ten miles from Pueblo, and surrounded the house.

There they took out S. D. Chastine, Barry Chastine and Frank Owsby and hanged them to trees near the house. At Pueblo they bound and gagged the jailer to prevent alarm and did the whole work so quietly as to raise no disturbance and they were all in their beds by morning, so that no trace can be found to any man who was away from home last night. They told the Pueblo jailer they selected this morning because of the incredulity of the people to-day to prevent the immediate success of any alarm.

There appears to be a very strong impression in the minds of those who watch the progress of affairs at the mouth of the Brazos river that the engineer in charge, Colonel Mansfield, is laboring to retard the removal of the bar instead of doing that which the government has intended. There can be no doubt that deep water can be secured on this bar, and the citizens of that section should lay their complaints where they might do some good. Colonel Mansfield has spoken positively as to the possibility of removing the bar, and unless he meets public expectation, based on his own opinions, somebody else should be placed in charge of the work. A double hanging, by Judge Lynch, which occurred last week in Comanche county, caused, so says the Chief, "a ripple" of excitement in Comanche. A country where such things stir the placid surface of public sentiment to the extent of "a ripple" must be a desirable place for nervous people, who value human life, to emigrate to. Small affairs will not annoy them. The poor devils who were hung had been charged—not convicted—of stealing cotton.—[Waco Examiner.

GIVE IT UP.

Statistics show that more than 30 per cent. of the negroes over 10 years old in northern states are unable to write, whereas the whites over 10 years old unable to write amount to less than 5 per cent. Still there is a great deal of stuff about discrimination against the negroes in the south in the matter of education. The per cent. of illiteracy among the negroes in the old free states is six times as great as among the whites, whereas it is less than three times as great in the old slave states. What might be the educational condition of the negro were the race as numerous in the north as in the south?—[Austin Statesman.

The democrats of congress should not bite at the bait of abolishing the internal revenue. There must be a sweeping reform in legislation all around, of which that will be only a part.—[Colorado Courier.

It is an old adage that minister's sons are generally good-for-nothing fellows. Texas leads the Union in crops this year. According to the United States crop reports Texas scores nothing below 90, and runs from that, the lowest, to 106, the highest. But there is not one in the whole list of thirty-eight states which has the general average given to Texas crops.—[Belton Reporter.

Congress will be in session only three months and the republicans will have to work like Trojans it they accomplish much in so short a time. They will have to come square down to business and stick to it. In their last hours of power they should acquit themselves well for the respect they owe to the country.—[Fort Worth Democrat.

THE COLOR LINE.

There is contention in St. Louis on what is called the color line. A Mrs Nash sends her two children to the white school. It is quite impossible to discern that these children are not white. The question has to be treated as one of pedigree. In that Mrs. Nash prevails, that is to say, the children are technically, as well as actually, white. But if they were not so, if it were ascertained that some remote ancestor of Mrs. Nash had been of African extraction her children would have been "bounced" and consigned to the school of negroes. To obviate the difficulty thus existing on either hand, might not schools be graduated? Might there not be a school, or department, for the negro, another for the mulatto, a third for the quadroon and higher types to that verge where both the sense and sentiment of the social perfection will cease to be shocked?—[San Antonio Express.

McGregor, Iowa, July 27.—Two freight trains collided four miles from here last night on the Milwaukee & St. Paul railway. Fireman M. Hubbard and two tramps were killed and several people were injured. The engines were locked together and most of the cars plunged over a high trestle work.

SHREVEPORT, LA., July 27.—About 9 o'clock this morning the Minden mail stage was robbed by two masked men, near Clark's Bayou, fifteen miles from here. As the time wore on and no party came the mob became impatient, and some cried, "Break the door in and bring them out." A few men, who were pretty well intoxicated, moved around urging a general attack, and succeeded in getting the crowd worked up. They walked up to the door of the jail and boldly asked for the prisoners. The door, which had been opened from within, was closed in their faces, and they fell back. After a half hour's work, Pettis and John Montgomery were pulled out through an opening in the top of a cell and handed over to the mob. A brand new rope was produced and thrown around the necks of the men. The mob then endeavored by blows, threats, and every means known to them to induce the wretches to confess.

"I am innocent, gentlemen!" cried Pettis, in an agonizing voice.

"You lie, — you; you know you did it!"

"I know I am going to die, but as God is my judge I am innocent," repeated Pettis.

Then there was a surging of the crowd in the small apartment, and a cry, "Take them out and hang them!" John Montgomery in the mean time was exclaiming, "I am innocent; I don't know anything!"

The workers of the mob were searching for Clementi, who could not be found. The cells were all opened by the use of a crowbar, and then it was discovered that Clementi was not in the jail. Pettis and Montgomery were then dragged down stairs and into the jail yard, the crowd looking for a good tree as they went along. The trees were all saplings, and a halt was made, during which a confession was sought to be extracted from Montgomery, but the man still protested his innocence.

"To the Court House yard!" some one cried, and other voices took it up. To the Court House yard the mob went, threatening and bullying the prisoners on their way, Lee Pettis repeating, "I am innocent: I am innocent."

The Court House yard was soon reached, and the crowd halted under a tall tree. Some nimble fellow climbed the tree and threw the end of the rope into a forked branch. A dozen hands caught the loose end, and John Montgomery was jerked off his feet. The poor wretch pleaded innocence, and a hundred voices called upon him to speak out and tell his story. He said: "I have no story to tell; I am innocent. I know no more about this matter than you." His voice was as weak as a woman's and as pathetic as a child's, but the infuriated mob hooted and yelled at him, telling him he was a dead man anyway and he might as well confess. "I am innocent," reiterated Montgomery. "Up he goes then," shouted those at the other end of the rope, and up he did go. His body was pulled up about four feet from the ground and kept there a full minute. The man was not strangled, but, being exhausted and weakened with fear, the men who held the rope let him down, and he was again asked to confess his guilt. The man could not speak at first, but laid limp upon the grass. After he recovered his breath he said:

"Gentlemen, I know I am dying, and I tell you I am as innocent as you are."

A cry for A. D. Bond, the father of the victim, was then given by the mob, and a big burly man pushed his way in. He stood beside the prisoner and asked him to tell if he was not in the school house on the afternoon of the outrage, but through all he maintained his ignorance of the guilty parties. The mob yelled for the immediate hanging of the prisoner. For an hour those about the man talked, bullied, stormed, and threatened, but the poor abject wretch repeatedly reiterated his innocence.

In the mean time Clementi had been found and was held by the mob on the other side of the yard. Cowering down with his head on his breast, his neck drawn in like a turtle's, he shook and shivered, and when goaded, chattered out his innocence. Lee Pettis was held with a rope round his neck and tortured also. He loudly and boldly proclaimed his innocence, and told the mob to go on and hang him.

Montgomery was about to be swung up again, when Mr. Bond cut the rope, and the prisoner was taken to one side of the yard and subjected to another series of questions. It was all in vain; the man who held the rope were unwilling to hang a man after his repeated declarations of innocence, and gradually their manners softened. Some one cried out, "Turn them loose." and in a few minutes the cry became general. The fringe of men on the outskirts of the crowd yelled, "Hang him." "Remember your families."

A light in the western part of the town drew attention away from the prisoners. A large barn was on fire, and a large portion of the crowd ran away to see it. The Prosecuting Attorney and the father of Miss Bond persuaded the rest to return the prisoners to the jail, and, after a consultation among the leaders, they were taken back to jail and placed in their cells. The prisoners are not in much danger now, as their steadfast denials had a good deal of weight with the mob.

An Easier Feeling.
SPRINGFIELD, Ill., August 12.—A dispatch from Tayloryville, Ill., says that the town is still greatly excited over the events of last night, but a reaction in public sentiment is fast taking place and much regret is expressed at the lawless proceedings of the mob in their efforts to lynch Montgomery, Pettis and Clementi. A Blue Mound special of the 22d inst. says: Emma Bond is dying, and her end cannot be a week distant. riley-anderson-greenville-1882-10-02.A6: Lou Griffin, a mulatto woman, and her child four months old, were brutally murdered in Austin Township, Greenville county, on Tuesday of last week. She and her husband lived on the farm of Dr. Crayton, though they had been separated for some time on account of an alleged too close intimacy between her and Riley Anderson, another colored man. On the 26th ultimo she had started to a place about eight miles distant, leaving about 8 o'clock. She was not again seen alive, but was found dead with her infant beside her on Wednesday about 12 o'clock by some white children. Her body was not above one mile from Dr. Crayton's farm and when found was "lying on her back with her head inclined to one side, with her arms extended and besmeared with blood, one bloody hand still clutching her apron." Severe wounds, the effects of heavy blows, were visible upon her forehead. The body of the child was on the right of the mother and its skull was terribly crushed. At the inquest the husband clearly proved an alibi and suspicion attached to Riley Anderson, the evidence being such as to warrant the jury in finding a verdict that Lou Griffin and her child "came to their death by strokes with a stick in the hands of Riley Anderson on the 26th of September, 1882." Sheriff Gilreath arrested Anderson and he was lodged in jail at Greenville. Anderson is a short heavy built man and has always borne an excellent character, being an industrious farmer. He has considerable property. He denies any knowledge of the murder and by reason of his past character many doubt his guilt.

riley-anderson-greenville-1882-10-02.A10:
Attempted Lynching.
We publish an account of the attempted lynching, in Greenville, of Riley Anderson. After a thorough search of the jail and yard without discovering the whereabouts of the prisoner the crowd proceeded up Main street to a point near the Opera House, and a squad of eight men were sent to wait upon Sheriff Gilreath. After repeated raps at the Sheriff's door that gentleman appeared, but was not surprised, as his visitors had been expected. They demanded to know the whereabouts of Riley Anderson, which information the Sheriff calmly but resolutely refused to give.

After much parleying the Sheriff went with the squad to where the crowd of about 100 were waiting. On his arrival there he found them a most determined throng, saying they would have the murderer at any cost. The Sheriff addressed them in a calm and determined voice, saying it was his duty as a officer of the law to protect the prisoner in his custody; that, having learned of their intentions, he had placed Anderson out of their reach, and assured them that their mission would be a fruitless one. Headvised them to return to their homes and let the law take its course, as the time for lynching had passed when Anderson was lodged in jail.

The speech of the Sheriff, who is immensely popular with the people of the county, had a wholesome effect and the crowd jocularly acknowledging that they had been outgeneraled by the Sheriff returned to the suburbs and scattered for their homes.

The Sheriff having received hints Monday of the intended lynching, removed Anderson from jail early Monday night, not without strategy, however. Finding several men hanging about the jail whom he suspected as spies, he engaged, apparently unconcerned, in conversation with them in front of the jail, while deputies departed with the prisoner Anderson through the back door. He was taken to the top of the cupola of the Court House, from which, under charge of two deputies, with an ague of fear and trembling, he witnessed the procession and heard the threats of the crowd who were bent on his hanging. In this elevated position the prisoner was kept till Tuesday morning, when he was quietly escorted to the train, and sent to Anderson.

Use of Pistols by the Police.
The shooting of the negro Smith by Policeman Martinez, should bring to public attention the danger of arming the police;—a pistol in the hands of a policeman is as dangerous as in the hands of a cow boy,—perhaps more so. Martinez, thought because he was a policeman he had a right to shoot down a flying thief, and yet, had he killed his victim, he would have been guilty of murder and been entitled to the honor of pulling hemp at the public expense; as it is, he will be subject to a charge of assault with intent to murder.

A policeman has no greater right to use his pistol upon a fellow-man than any other person has. He must only use it in self defense, and then strictly under the conditions of any other unofficial person; in making an arrest the policeman is the aggressor and should be careful to only use more force necessary to perform his duty.
The only excuse for sheriffs and other officers carrying deadly weapons, is that they may possibly encounter desperate men, who carry arms and would resist peaceable arrest.

Deputy Sheriff Wm. Mulvenon Brings the Murderer Back from Kansas.
Last night Deputy Sheriff Mulvenon returned from Larnard, Pawnee county, Kansas; with Blind Jim, the notorious Flagstaff murderer, and lodged him in the county jail.

Jas. Packerson, alias Blind Jim, is charged with the killing of F. N. Stone, an A. & P. railroad contractor, at Flagstaff, on the 6th of July. Immediately after the murder Jim fled the country, although it was reported that the citizens of Flagstaff had hanged him and his partner. From Flagstaff he made his way east to Pawnee county, Kansas, where his father and step-mother reside. The authorities there got an inkling that Jim was wanted in this section, and telegraphed asking what they should do. Word was sent back to hold him, and he was immediately arrested. The Larnard officials, knowing that they had a desperate criminal to deal with kept him handcuffed and guarded by two men from the time he was arrested until Mr. Mulvenon arrived and relieved them of further responsibility. When Mr. Mulvenon went to get his prisoner the sheriff at Larnard seem-surprised that one man should come so far and undertake to convey back to Arizona alone such a desperate character as Jim was known to be, but our plucky official put the shackles on his prisoner and started for Prescott. At Albuquerque he learned that attempts would be made by Jim's friends to rescue him, and also that parties out along the road were determined to lynch him. Mr. Mulvenon requested the conductor to have the telegraph operator hold all dispatches until he got through, so that those who were waiting for him could not be informed of his movements. At Pittman Valley a party of men had gathered for the purposed of assisting Jim on a prospecting trip into the "sweet subsequently," but Sheriff Mulvenon got off at Volunteer with his prisoner, took a private conveyance and cut across the country, arriving in Prescott last night. The prisoner will have a hearing as soon as witnesses arrive from Flagstaff. Mr. Mulvenon deserves great credit for the satisfactory manner in which he accomplished his mission.

NEWBUROH, N. Y., February 14. Jonah Tompkins, residing at Tilke's hill, eight miles from Cold Spring, was murdered yesterday by his brother-in-law, Curtis Christian. Early in the morning the men set out together to buy cows and in the evening Christian returned and announced to his wife he had murdered Tompkins, stating where the body could be found. He then attacked his wife, but was overpowered and fled from the house. A search was made and the body found where indicated with the head crushed in by a stone. The indications are that a terrible struggle took place. The murderer is not yet arrested and it is believed has committed suicide. Supposed rivalry regarding the father-in-law's property was the cause of the crime.

KANAS CITY, Mo., February 14. The contemplated robbery of the Missouri Pacific train, due here at 8:40 to-night, was frustrated by the Kansas City police. It seems that seven men, all notorious characters of this city, formed a plan for the contemplated robbery some three months ago, but the final arrangements were only completed a few days ago, and to-night was set as the time. The place where the train was to be stopped was about five miles east of here. The police got wind of the affair sometime ago and have carefully nursed it. At 4 o'clock this afternoon five officers proceeded to the spot where the robbery was to take place and concealed themselves. The robbers soon appeared on the ground and cautiously began preparations for their work. A pile of ties and railroad iron was piled at the side of the track which they intended to use to stop the train. The officers pounced upon them and took in four of them, three making good their escape. These the officers hope to corral yet to-night. On the gang were found a number of revolvers, shot guns, masks, and lancers. The names of the gang arrested are Jas. Nooman, Thos. O'Shea, Pat Hanley and Peter Speer. They admit that they intended to commit the robbery as charged and have given the officers full details of their plans, when it was conceived and how it has been worked up. One of the gang undoubtedly gave his comrades away to the authorities.

CHICAGO, February 14.—Johnny Lamb, who has been on trial once for the robbery of Jaffrey's store three years ago, and twice for the murder of Policeman Race after the robbery, the last trial having been in progress several weeks, was to-day acquitted. As he passed out of the jail a free man, the inmates gave him a great ovation. He is now the greatest hero of Chicago crooks.

Hanged for Theft.
ATHENS, Ga., Feb. 14.—An account of one of the most extraordinary lynchings on record is just received from Guinnet County, this State, the victim of the mob's vengeance being a negro named Wm. Smeal, whose only crime was that of stealing horses. The negro was employed to work on the plantation of Mr. Tom Dillard, a prominent planter, and was said to be an industrious man, with a bad reputation, however, as a thief.

Some time last week a horse was stolen in the neighborhood, and suspicion was at once fixed upon the negro. So, upon Sunday night, a number of men organized themselves and resolved to inflict what they considered proper punishment upon the suspected man. They proceeded in a body to Mr. Dillard's place, broke open the cabin where the negro made his home, and carried him out.

They then took turns in beating the poor wretch until he confessed the theft and piloted the mob to where the stolen horse was tied up in the woods. But the negro's punishment did not end with this, as the mod at once procured a trace chain from a wagon, put it around the miserable man's neck and hanged him to a black-jack tree, near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville Road, where he was found hanging yesterday morning dead. There is much indignation over this atrocious act, and the perpetrators will be made to feel the law if they can be discovered.
